thesis: The GAME matrix assigns work by comparative human and computer difficulty.
summary: Give covers routine work; accelerate covers difficult research and analysis; integrate covers creative or strategic collaboration; no AI reserves human presence for leadership, persuasion, coaching and networking. For automation Martell asks whether a task repeats, follows rules and returns more time than it costs. For collaborative work he retains human taste, vision and care, illustrating iterative drafting followed by a designer’s work.

insights.title: Allocate tasks by comparative difficulty
insights.explanation: The framework has give, accelerate, integrate and no-AI categories, with human presence as a deliberate outcome.
insights.quote: the person who understands the problem the best they'll actually win

insights.explanation: He explicitly rejects a long setup for a tiny recurring task.

review_status: Codex editorial draft; complete local transcript read; claims not independently verified
synthesis_method: Direct Codex extraction from complete local transcript; exact quotations verified locally
context_and_limits: A heuristic matrix, not a measured capability boundary or proof specialists are unnecessary. Fixed 10/80/10 work shares are suggested roles, not audited time savings. AI pattern analysis, legal review and personal prioritization can be wrong. Some narration says the I quadrant is easy despite its defined hard/hard axis; follow the explicit definition and describe the slip. Claims that AI cannot perform any named interpersonal act are overbroad.
review_changes: Adds the setup-cost test, specific boundaries of collaboration and the distinction between idea generation, human selection and final specialist execution.
